result.summary: Pausanias walks the road Apheta from the Spartan market-place and lists its sights. He explains the names Apheta and Booneta, then notes shrines, hero-chapels and tombs, and the Scias with its round building.

scenes.title: Apheta, Booneta and Celeuthea
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains the road's name through Icarius' race for Penelope's hand, compares Danaus' race, and explains how Booneta was bought with oxen. He also tells of Athene Celeuthea's temples.

scenes.title: Shrines and tombs along Apheta
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists hero-chapels, temples and tombs along the road, including Hellenium, the tomb of Talthybius and the royal tombs. He tells of Talthybius' wrath after the murder of Darius' envoys.

scenes.title: The Scias and round building
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Scias, built by Theodorus, where Timotheus' harp was hung up, and the round building by Epimenides.

alias_notes.explanation: Title given by Odysseus to Athene's statue.

notable_quotes.reason: Shows Pausanias' view of primitive barter before coinage.

analysis.text: Place names are explained through legend and history, linking Spartan topography to heroic myth and the Persian Wars.
The passage records Spartan cults, tombs and the Talthybius story about Persian envoys, reflecting how Greeks remembered the Persian Wars.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias cites sailors' reports about India, showing his use of oral sources.

language_notes.text: Apheta means 'starting-place' (from a verb meaning to let go), the point where runners were released; Booneta means 'ox-bought'.
The clause 'that Odysseus won the prize is clear' is awkwardly inserted; Pausanias means it is agreed Odysseus won Penelope by this race.
The 'atrocious crime' is the murder of their husbands, the sons of Aegyptus, on their wedding night by the Danaids, daughters of Danaus.
'In the lump' means unminted metal, weighed out rather than counted as coins.
Refers to the Greek alliance against Xerxes' Persian invasion of 480 BC; Hellenium is explained as their council-place.
Darius' heralds asking for earth and water were killed in Sparta (and Athens); Talthybius was Agamemnon's herald, honoured at Sparta, so his anger fell on both cities.
Theodorus of Samos was a famous early craftsman, credited with inventing iron casting or modelling.
Timotheus of Miletus, a musician, was censured for adding strings to the traditional seven-string lyre, which Spartans saw as corrupting music.

context_notes.text: Icarius was Penelope's father and a Spartan; Odysseus (Ulysses) won her hand before going to Troy.
Pausanias cites Indian trade as a parallel for barter; he is reporting sailors' accounts, not his own observation.
Celeuthea means 'of the roads' or 'path-making', an epithet of Athene as guide of travellers.
The Eurypontidæ were one of Sparta's two royal houses; Sparta always had two kings.
Thermopylæ was the 480 BC pass where Leonidas and his Spartans died resisting Xerxes.
The 'great Mother' is the Asian goddess Cybele, whose cult was widespread in Greece.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias interposes his own judgement ('I think'), showing his habit of weighing traditions and drawing comparisons.
Pausanias contrasts primitive barter with later coinage, giving the odd house-price in oxen historical depth.
Talthybius' wrath falling unevenly on Spartans and Athenians, with Miltiades' family suffering, shows a divine retribution that is oddly personal.
